Given this, it seems important to acknowledge that the online data does contribute meaningful improvement, or otherwise recognize that the overall effectiveness of the proposed model may be limited.

**Response [Training with differing team sizes]** 
We have run additional results for MLPO  applied to different team sizes, namely 2 and 4 agents (results for 3 agents are from our original draft). We ran these experiments on homogenous teams consisting of Gemma, Qwen, or Llama, since altering the number of agents with diverse teams introduces the confounder of _which_ model to remove or add.

2. Although there is a general trend that using more models (4 vs 3 or 2) is better, however we would expect to see performance drop after a certain point. Based the above experiments, we speculate that this decrease would likely occur around 5 or 6 agents.

- _Although training only a single leader model reduces training costs, the overall collaboration quality may be constrained by the leader’s capability. If the leader LLM’s task ability is weak, it could perform worse than untrained agents debating directly or a single untrained agent answering alone._

**Response [Sensitivity to choice of leader]** We agree that MLPO's performance depends on the strength of the leader model; we actually highlight this point in Section 4.4 and Appendix C. This sensitivity is not unique to MLPO, as any post-training-based multi-agent method (ACC-Collab, SCoRe, SelectLLM, etc.) will exhibit the same dependency. That said, we note that the dependence may be more significant in our case since the leader is in a "centralized" role and thus has a greater influence on the process. Importantly, across all three benchmarks, MLPO still consistently outperforms baselines (Tables 1, 7, 8); in two cases where our method struggles to beat untrained agents (namely Gemma and Llama leaders on MMLU), no training-based baseline can outperform untrained diverse MAD (Appendix C, Tables 7, 8). We also note that the flip side of this sensitivity is true; stronger leaders would also be more robust to a weak agent team (similar to observations made in Figure 5). 

We fully agree that this is an important point to be made more explicitly and thus we have added the following to our conclusion on line 497:
> Further, MLPO relies on a central leader model, and is more sensitive to the leader's efficacy (compared with other multi-agent approaches that do not utilize a central agent); as such, we recommend using a model with comparable strength to the agent team.

--- 
- _During training, “easy tasks” (those with a team accuracy ≥ 75%) are filtered out to focus on the leader’s coordination skills. This 75% threshold is heuristic and lacks theoretical grounding or systematic validation._

**Response [Filtering Easy Takes]** The 75% threshold follows difficulty-filtering strategies used in prior works on GRPO-based training, e.g., [improving Data Efficiency for LLM Fine Tuning](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2506.05316), [DAPO](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2503.14476), [SKywork R1V2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2504.16656). In our experiments, we observed that filtering out "easy" questions improved MLPO performance (Appendix B.3, Table 6). While some prior works use dynamic (online) filtering, we have a unique advantage in that agent-team solutions are computed before training. Thus, we can use these pre-computed responses to gauge the difficulty of each question (removing the need to compute difficulty during training). The most straightforward way is to set a hard threshold. In our early experiments we tested several thresholds and found that 75% was consistently the best performing threshold. As this filtering is informed by prior work, we view finding the "optimal" filtering value as out of the scope of our work. We merely wanted to outline that difficulty filtering helps in improving performance.

- _According to Figure 2, the multi-agent team is not generating new data during MLPO. Why is this setting advocated?_

**Response [Agent Responses During Training]** This is a great question and strikes at one of our key motivations, namely the practicality of training. Requiring 4 models to be held in memory while performing an already expensive training (RL-based training), would significantly increase the overhead of our method. We find that pre-computing agent responses, rather than computing them online, still results in quite high performance (as shown by our results). Additionally, we also provide a variant of MLPO that uses an additional step where agent responses are recomputed after the leader provides a response (MLPO+). We find that this additional step can result in better performance (Table 2), but the gains are quite minimal (1%-4%). Thus, lending more strength to the idea that one needs only use round 0 responses during training, which is already sufficient to beat consistently beat or tie with all baselines across each of the datasets and models we study (Tables 1, 7, 8).

- _SFT transparency & potential advantage. Appendix A.1 describes how the SFT data are constructed (synthetic backtracking/self‑correction), but omits crucial statistics: dataset size, token counts, domain/source mix, and sampling rules (p. 17). This makes it hard to judge how much of the gain stems from SFT itself vs. MLPO, and it obscures fairness vs. baselines that may not receive equivalent SFT._


**Response [MLPO gains from SFT]** We agree that isolating the effects of SFT on MLPO is important! This is precisely why we provide results for pure SFT, MLPO without SFT, and MLPO with SFT in our main results (Table 1). In this table, the row "SFT Leader" refers to a leader trained only on the SFT data, "SFT + MLPO Leader" refers to MLPO with the initial SFT step, and "MLPO Leader" refers to MLPO without this initial SFT. We find that while this SFT step increases performance, the majority of the performance is obtained from MLPO itself, for example, on BBH the untrained leader attains accuracy 0.764, the SFT leader the MLPO leader attains 0.865, and SFT + MLPO Leader attains 0.882.
 


**Response [Sampling SFT data]** 
We described SFT sampling in Appendix E.3 of our draft. However, in light of this question, we have added additional clarifications to this Appendix E.3, and added details in Appendix D.3. For completeness we reiterate these details here. To teach the leader model natural backtracking and self-correction behavior, we construct a supervised fine-tuning (SFT) dataset comprising synthetic completions that mimic realistic reasoning failures followed by recovery.

For each dataset, we begin by running our untrained multi-agent pipeline to collect 16 distinct completions from the leader for each agent team generation. We discard examples where all completions are incorrect or correct. For the remaining examples, we randomly select one correct and one incorrect leader completion. These are then used to construct a prompt that asks an untrained leader model to imitate a reasoning process that starts with plausible but flawed logic (using the incorrect trajectory), then backtracks and self-corrects to reach the correct answer (using the correct trajectory). We then filter out any remaining examples where the backtracking did not yield a correct final answer. The generated backtracked completions form the core of our SFT dataset. We have also included an example of the backtracked completion used for SFT in Appendix E.3. We use an identical process for GRPO, without the agent team involvement and with a higher sample budget to ensure a similar number of examples are used for both methods (32).



**Response [Training Statistics]**
Below, we have added a table outlining the SFT training data statistics for both MLPO and GRPO in our paper. Note that these are the only two methods that receive an initial SFT step (SCoRE has its own two-phase training, ACC-Collab combines SFT and DPO during training). For both MLPO and GRPO, the training data has roughly the same number of training examples. We note that while the prompt length of the SFT data is much larger for MLPO (which is masked in the loss), the response length is fairly similar (which is not masked in the loss). This table is also added to our draft (Table 15).

- _Effect of filtering “easy” tasks. Since §3.2 filters tasks where ≥75% of 4K agent responses are correct (p. 5) and Table 6 (p. 23) shows benefits, were analogous difficulty controls applied to baselines? If not, can you provide results without filtering to isolate MLPO’s contribution?_

**Response [Difficulty Filtering and Baselines]** We apply the same filtering to the RL baselines, namely GRPO and SCoRE, but not to the other baselines as it results in worse performance for the other baselines. Moreover, some baselines, like ACC-Collab, have their own filtering scheme.

The filtering has a two-fold benefit for MLPO. Firstly, since MLPO uses GRPO-style training, "easy" questions will frequently yield an advantage term of 0 (since the reward for each rollout is identical). Secondly, "easy" questions have the potential to teach the leader a degenerate signal of simply agreeing with the majority of agents. We are not sure why the filtering results in worse performance for baselines like ACC-Collab and SelectLLM although this is beyond the scope of our work. 



- _Zero‑shot comparison tokens. In §4.2.3 (Fig. 4, p. 7), does the Zero‑shot GRPO baseline see the same total training tokens as the SFT+MLPO leader? If not, can you provide a token‑matched comparison?_

**Response [Token Normalized Training vs Sample Normalized Training]** To the best of our knowledge, token-normalized training comparisons are not common in multi-agent training papers (we are not aware of a single multi-agent training paper that makes such a comparison), or even in GRPO-based training papers such as [DAPO](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2503.14476) or [Dr.GRPO](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2503.20783), which provides their comparisons in terms of the number of training steps (MLPO and GRPO share the same number of training steps in our setting). In our experiment,s both MLPO and GRPO expose the model to the same number of examples (resulting in the same number of updates). However, MLPO almost certainly exposes the model to more tokens; this is a key advantage of MLPO, not an asymmetry of our experimental comparisons. Because MLPO uses the joint of questions q and agents' solutions S, the data domain can be far richer than using the questions alone. MLPO is implicitly a data augmentation method that allows multiple training samples $(q, S_1)$, $(q, S_2)$, etc, to stem from the same question q by leveraging different agent solutions $S_i$.

summary.value: This paper proposes a new concept called a multi-agent leader, then proposes a training method to tune the leader agent, aiming to improve the summarization and answer-seeking ability from multi-agent system rollouts. They test their proposed approach in three benchmarks and achieve a significant improvement compared to baselines.

strengths.value:
- The paper introduces a novel and practical hierarchical multi-agent framework. Its main advantage is its computational efficiency, as it only requires training a single "leader" model while coordinating a team of fixed, untrained peer agents. This significantly reduces the training cost and complexity compared to approaches that require co-training multiple specialized models.
- The proposed Multi-agent guided Leader Policy Optimization (MLPO) is a novel contribution. It provides an effective method for training the leader to evaluate and synthesize diverse responses from the agent team without needing auxiliary value networks or explicit agent feedback, which simplifies the overall training pipeline.

weaknesses.value:
- The benchmark (MMLU, BBH, MATH) does not seem to be related to a multi-agent system. They are knowledge-intensive tasks. I hope the author can provide some clarification on why they chose these benchmarks.
- Figure 2 seems not to be related to Figure 1, where in Figure 1, the data generation pipeline is online, i.e., the leader's feedback will return to the multi-agent system for new rollouts. If the leader's feedback cannot return to the multi-agent system, the leader will be degraded to a summarizer, which reduces the novelty of the task.
- The effectiveness of the framework appears to be sensitive to the choice of the leader model. The authors note in their analysis (Section 4.4) that while MLPO shows gains, the performance increase was less significant when using Gemma-2 and Llama-3.1 as leaders compared to Qwen-2.5. This suggests the method may require a highly capable base model (like Qwen-2.5) to act as an effective leader.

- _"Implicit Data Augmentation" vs. Algorithmic Novelty In response to the query about token count fairness, the authors state that "MLPO almost certainly exposes the model to more tokens" and characterize this as a benefit of "implicit data augmentation."To me, this confirms that the performance advantage may not stem from the superior design of the optimization mechanism (the RL/GRPO component), but simply from the fact that the model consumes significantly more synthetic reasoning tokens from agents during training than the baselines. This aligns more with the paradigm of computation-heavy Knowledge Distillation or extensive Data Augmentation rather than a novel Multi-Agent RL contribution. If the gain disappears when baselines are allowed to "read" an equivalent volume of synthetic reasoning traces (e.g., via simple SFT or DPO on the same agent outputs), then the value of the complex MLPO reinforcement learning loop is diminished._


**Response [Algorithmic Novelty]** A key advantage of MLPO is that it allows multiple training examples to stem from the same question, thus allowing us to extend our training data so long as we can generate possible agent solutions. This ability to get more out of a given fixed training set is a key advantage of MLPO. The way in which MLPO extends these examples is itself a key novelty; for each question $q$, MLPO exposes the leader to $k$ different possible solution sets $S_1, …, S_k$, yielding examples $(q, S_1), …, (q, S_k)$. This exposure to multiple possible solutions allows the leader to better explore the space of solutions at training time. This goes beyond mere token exposure and represents a novel data augmentation that not only improves the model’s performance as a leader, but also as a single model functioning in a zero-shot setting with no team (see Table 1).


- _Marginal Gains vs. High Complexity The rebuttal breakdown reveals that the "SFT Leader" alone already achieves strong performance (e.g., 0.865 on BBH), while the full "SFT + MLPO Leader" improves this to 0.882.This yields a marginal gain of . However, achieving this requires a highly complex and computationally expensive pipeline: Generation (4K proposals)  Filtering  SFT Construction  SFT Training  GRPO RL Training._


**Response [Gains from SFT are minimal]** There appears to be some confusion so we have provided a table quoting the performance, from our paper, of the untrained leader, MLPO with SFT-only leader, MLPO with RL-only leader, and MLPO with an SFT+RL leader (our main method). In the table below we see that the performance of the SFT-only leader is almost equivalent to that of the untrained leader, while the performance, **implying that the gains from SFT are minimal, and that the bulk of the improvement comes from the RL-stage of MLPO**. 


For example, in the table below, the SFT-only leader has identical performance with the untrained leader on BBH, while the MLPO-only leader has 10% higher accuracy.

The method appears to be an inefficient way to squeeze out small performance gains compared to the robust SFT baseline._

**Response [Training Time]** While MLPO requires more GPU hours for training, the increased performance is clear: MLPO beats, or occasionally ties with, all training baselines. We agree that for some users the increased training time may not be acceptable, but for those with additional compute, MLPO offers a straightforward means of boosting performance.


- _Token-Matched Baseline: The most critical missing piece is a baseline that is trained on the same volume of agent-generated tokens but using a simpler objective (e.g., standard SFT or DPO on the correct agent trajectories without the RL loop). This would isolate whether the gain comes from the training signal (MLPO) or just the data scale._


**Response [Token-Matched Baseliness]**  As mentioned previously, training with equal numbers of tokens is not a common evaluation metric. We are not aware of any similar works that make token matched comparisons (e.g., DAPO and Dr. GRPO both do not provide this evaluation metric). It would appear that the reviewer is also not aware of any such works, as they declined to provide any works that make this comparison.

Moreover, they can document baseline tuning budgets; where margins are small (e.g., MATH), report sensitivity to temperature/top‑p, number of rounds, and aggregation schemes; include paired‑seed significance tests (Table 1)._

**Response [Additional Analysis]** Thank you for the suggestions, in particular the inference time token-normalized comparisons! We have added these to our draft (Appendix B.1, Line 956, and Table 3) and also provide results below. 

_Sensitivity in slim cases_: We fully acknowledge that in some cases (for Llama and Gemma) our improvement over the baselines is slim. However, we note two things; firstly, we consistently beat all baselines (and occasionally tie), and secondly, for Qwen (a model known to be more effective with RL-based post-training) we consistently see quite large improvements over the baselines. 


_Number of rounds:_ We would like to highlight that, we actually do have experiments with varying rounds in the main paper and refer the reviewer to Figure 3, 7 (full version of 3), and 9. 

_Aggregation Schemes:_ In terms of aggregation schemes, we would also like to direct the reviewer to Table 1 and Figure 3 of the main paper. Here we compare various aggregation methods, including Deferral (trained to always defer to one agent in the team), SelectLLM (from a large pool of different LLMs, decide for each input/query which subset of models to query), as well as Majority vote (Section 4.2.2).

_Token Normalized Inference_: Below, we provide token-normalized comparisons for each method after 2 rounds of inference (rounds 0 and 1). For this experiment, each method is allowed to generate $k$ answers until the token budget is reached (if $k=0$, i.e., one answer exceeds the token budget, the answer is counted as wrong). We include our trained leader both with the agent team (MLPO Leader) and without the team (MLPO No Team). We make two important observations about these results:
1. For all larger budgets (10k and above), the MLPO Leader consistently beats all baselines. 
2. For these larger token budget ,the MLPO leader without the team consistently beats a model trained only with GRPO. 

We acknowledge that in settings of a lower inference budget (5k tokens or less), single model solutions like GRPO may be preferable, but for larger budgets (7500 or above) our method is preferable.

For clarity, we also provide them here. For GRPO, we use an identical setup, i.e., an initial SFT step with backtracking data (using the same number of examples as MLPO) followed by an RL step. ACC-Collab does not make use of such a pre-training set, since this method uses a mix of SFT and DPO and requires a specific data format during training. **Response [SelectLLM Budget]** We apologize for the confusion. SelectLLM is unique compared to the other baselines since it is the only baseline with majority-vote baked in; it intakes a sample budget $k$, question $q$ and collection of models $M_1, \ldots, M_n$, and determines how to distribute the sample budget over the $n$ models. For a fair comparison, we set $k$ to the total number of samples used by our method in our two settings. For all results in Section 4.2.2 (where we investigate sample-normalized majority vote) SelectLLM uses a 40-vote budget in order to match the total sample budget used by all methods in this section. Outside of Section 4.2.2, SelectLLM is given a budget of 20 total samples in order to match the number of samples used by our method (3 agents + 1 leader, over 5 rounds).  We have clarified this in the updated version of our draft (Appendix D.1 Line 1428).

We have provided updated results in the draft (Appendix B.2, Line 1178, Line 1223, Table 5, and Table 6) and also reported them here. 1. Leader performance is quite robust to the number of agents, although we do see a decrease as $K$ becomes large (5 or 6). This is likely due to either an overload of the leader's context, or an innate susceptibility  of LLMs to agree with majority opinions as more opinions are presented (as outlined in these papers  [[1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2410.12428), [2](https://openreview.net/pdf?id=sy7eSEXdPC)])
2. For some weaker teams (e.g., Llama on MATH) it is better to deploy the leader as a solo agent (or with a diverse team as outlined in our main text). This lends more support to our hypothesis that diverse teams are generally the most effective.

A key focus of our work was on keeping training and deployment practical (e.g., reducing the number of models and generations required during training, or the ability to deploy our leader without the team at inference time). summary.value: The paper presents a hierarchical setup where one main “leader” model coordinates a small group of helper agents. Only the leader is trained, while the others stay fixed. The leader first goes through supervised fine-tuning using synthetic data, then is further improved with a GRPO-like reinforcement objective (called MLPO). During testing, the leader communicates with the helper agents for T rounds to combine their responses into a final answer. On the task BBH, MATH, and MMLU, the approach reports gains over training‑free and training‑based baselines, and intriguingly the trained leader also improves in zero‑shot (solo) mode (Table 1; Fig. 4).

strengths.value:
1. Train one coordinator that reads multiple agent drafts and outputs a consolidated answer; the inference workflow is well depicted (Fig. 1 on p. 3; Fig. 2 on p. 4).
2. On all three benchmarks the leader trained with SFT+MLPO outperforms strong single‑ and multi‑agent baselines (Table 1 on p. 6).
3. Analyses of team diversity (heterogeneous vs. homogeneous), exposure to alternative solutions, and information sharing (reasoning vs. final answers) provide insight (Appx B.2–B.3; Fig. 11–12 on pp. 21–22).

weaknesses.value:
1. The evaluation scope is relatively narrow, which lacks evidence of generality. Experiments cover only BBH, MMLU, MATH with 7–9B models; there is no evidence for code, retrieval/tool use, long‑context, or multilingual settings. Claims about “collaborative reasoning” need diverse tasks; current evidence mainly supports multiple‑choice and math settings in English. Other works on the same topic, such as Mixture-of-Agents [1] and ACC-Collab [2], usually cover a wider range of task types or provide more detailed comparative analyses to better support their claims about the generality of “collaborative reasoning.”

2. Although the paper trains only a single “leader,” its inference protocol requires a team of K=3 agents and T=5 sequential interaction rounds (leader–agents–leader …), which implies ~20 generations per query. The main text fixes T=5 (Sec. 3.1) and compares methods under a ceiling of “<= 40 generations with majority vote” (Fig. 3; Appx. Fig. 7), but it does not report token‑normalized or time‑normalized efficiency (e.g., wall‑clock latency, total prompt+completion tokens, or throughput) for the proposed method versus baselines. Appendix B.3 lists training hardware/hyper‑parameters but likewise omits inference latency/throughput; the conclusion explicitly acknowledges increased context lengths, higher inference compute, and reduced parallelizability due to sequential leader–agent interactions. Together, these omissions prevent a rigorous cost–quality comparison.

Thank the authors for the detailed rebuttal and for providing the requested statistics on compute and training data. While I appreciate the transparency, the new information reinforces my initial concerns regarding the source of the performance gains and the efficiency of the proposed method. 

I have decided to maintain my score based on the following two key reasons:

1. "Implicit Data Augmentation" vs. Algorithmic Novelty
In response to the query about token count fairness, the authors state that "MLPO almost certainly exposes the model to more tokens" and characterize this as a benefit of "implicit data augmentation."To me, this confirms that the performance advantage may not stem from the superior design of the optimization mechanism (the RL/GRPO component), but simply from the fact that the model consumes significantly more synthetic reasoning tokens from agents during training than the baselines. This aligns more with the paradigm of computation-heavy Knowledge Distillation or extensive Data Augmentation rather than a novel Multi-Agent RL contribution. If the gain disappears when baselines are allowed to "read" an equivalent volume of synthetic reasoning traces (e.g., via simple SFT or DPO on the same agent outputs), then the value of the complex MLPO reinforcement learning loop is diminished.


2. Marginal Gains vs. High Complexity
The rebuttal breakdown reveals that the "SFT Leader" alone already achieves strong performance (e.g., 0.865 on BBH), while the full "SFT + MLPO Leader" improves this to 0.882.This yields a marginal gain of $\sim1.7\%$. However, achieving this requires a highly complex and computationally expensive pipeline: Generation (4K proposals) $\rightarrow$ Filtering $\rightarrow$ SFT Construction $\rightarrow$ SFT Training $\rightarrow$ GRPO RL Training.

Given the high GPU-hours reported in the rebuttal (e.g., MLPO requires 172.2h on MMLU vs. significantly less for inference-time baselines or simpler training), the cost-benefit ratio is not favorable. The method appears to be an inefficient way to squeeze out small performance gains compared to the robust SFT baseline.

Suggestions for Future Improvement:

To clearly demonstrate the value of MLPO in future revisions, I suggest the following:

Token-Matched Baseline: The most critical missing piece is a baseline that is trained on the same volume of agent-generated tokens but using a simpler objective (e.g., standard SFT or DPO on the correct agent trajectories without the RL loop). This would isolate whether the gain comes from the training signal (MLPO) or just the data scale.

Efficiency Analysis: Investigate if the pipeline can be simplified. For instance, can the initial SFT phase be removed, or can the number of agent proposals needed for the RL phase be drastically reduced? Showing that MLPO works efficiently with a smaller "token budget" would strengthen the algorithmic claim.

Disentangling Reasoning vs. Aggregation: The paper claims the leader learns to "coordinate." However, since it sees full reasoning traces, it might just be learning to select the longest/most complex answer. An analysis on whether the leader is actually performing reasoning aggregation versus simple heuristic selection would add depth to the analysis.

- _The evaluation scope is relatively narrow, which lacks evidence of generality. Experiments cover only BBH, MMLU, MATH with 7–9B models; there is no evidence for code, retrieval/tool use, long‑context, or multilingual settings. Claims about “collaborative reasoning” need diverse tasks; current evidence mainly supports multiple‑choice and math settings in English. Other works on the same topic, such as Mixture-of-Agents [1] and ACC-Collab [2], usually cover a wider range of task types or provide more detailed comparative analyses to better support their claims about the generality of “collaborative reasoning.”_

**Response [Evaluation Scope]** We agree that adding additional benchmarks and model sizes would broaden the scope of work; however, we do study 3 benchmarks which cover a wide range of topics (BBH and MMLU are constructed from a mixture of many domains, and MATH covers open-ended mathematical reasoning). We train and evaluate a Qwen leader on teams of size 2, 3, and 4 (originally we presented results for size 3). We observe that generally larger teams yield better results, but the diverse team of 3 still consistently outperforms any homogeneous team of size 4. 
We also evaluate our leader trained on 3 agents with teams of varying sizes (0 to 6 agents). Leader performance is generally robust to the number of agents, with slight degradation for larger team sizes (likely due to context overload or majority-drift), and in some weak-team settings it is best to deploy the leader solo (Appendix B.2, Line 1168, Table 5, Line 1222, Table 7).

summary.value: This paper proposes a hierarchical multi-agent framework that trains a single leader LLM to coordinate several untrained companion agents, thereby reducing training costs while improving collaborative reasoning performance. Specifically, the paper introduces MLPO (Multi-agent guided Leader Policy Optimization). It first constructs a set of examples featuring self-correction/backtracking and uses SFT to enhance the leader’s abilities in aggregation, error correction, and backtracking. Then, within the GRPO framework, it treats the agents’ solutions as additional training context to directly optimize the leader model’s capability to evaluate and synthesize multiple answers. Experimental results show that, in multi-agent LLM systems, training only a flexible leader enables efficient and effective collaborative reasoning. Moreover, the trained leader model also achieves performance gains when deployed as a single model.

strengths.value:
1. Training only a single leader LLM to cooperate among several untrained companion agents significantly reduces training and maintenance costs, yet preserves the benefits of collaboration.
2. The paper introduces the MLPO training framework: construct SFT data to enhance the model’s self-correction ability, and directly optimize the leader under the GRPO framework—resulting in a relatively simple training process.
3. The trained leader model can operate in both “team collaboration” and “single-model” modes, indicating that the learned aggregation/correction strategies transfer to general reasoning ability.

weaknesses.value:
1. The experiments are conducted with a collaboration setting of K = 3 agents, without verifying the effectiveness of the proposed method as the number of untrained agents increases. Since MLPO treats untrained agents as part of the environment, increasing their number would make the environment more complex.
2. Although training only a single leader model reduces training costs, the overall collaboration quality may be constrained by the leader’s capability. If the leader LLM’s task ability is weak, it could perform worse than untrained agents debating directly or a single untrained agent answering alone.
3. During training, “easy tasks” (those with a team accuracy ≥ 75%) are filtered out to focus on the leader’s coordination skills. This 75% threshold is heuristic and lacks theoretical grounding or systematic validation.
4. It remains unclear whether the trained leader exhibits strong cross-team and cross-task generalization. For example, can a leader trained with one team configuration effectively guide a different team of agents? Can a leader trained on one task domain provide strong leadership on related tasks?
